preamble: Six lengthy across solutions are 17 11s and their clues are partial.

clue.text: Duet formed by man in post's to get better

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside the second

parts.note: a post is a job; the possessive supplies the S

indicators.note: letters that are formed into something are being rearranged into a new shape

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
he is any man
to cure is to get someone better

explanation.surface: Two singers team up with a man in post, hoping to make things better.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says this clue is only wordplay, so no definition appears. 'Post's' must be split: the reworked duet and the man go between its first letter and the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this is his last novel, about the stonemason Jude Fawley.

clue.text: Driver's get-together during excursion

indicators.note: something happening during an event sits within its span, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a jaunt is a short pleasure trip
things that mesh come together and fit

explanation.surface: A motorist mentions a social gathering held on an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get-together' looks like a noun for a party, but here it is the verb MESH. The 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: James Hunt was the British racing driver who won the 1976 Formula One world championship.

clue.text: Princess and queen got together and got fouled

parts.note: Diana, Princess of Wales, was widely known as Di
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen
tied means joined or bound together

explanation.surface: Two royal women meet up and somehow end up in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'and' is part of the charade sequence; the second joins wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that was dirtied has been made filthy, which is exactly what being fouled means.

clue.text: Firsts of the worst of our time

indicators.note: firsts are the leading items, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lament that our era has produced the very worst things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of our time' reads as one phrase about the present age; only 'time' is the definition, and 'of our' supplies letters untouched.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-four is a musical time signature, two crotchet beats in every bar, as used for marches.

clue.text: Another 17 11 (3,6,2,3,6)'s musical opening

indicators.note: the hidden title begins with RETURN, and to return is to go back the way you came
an opening is just the front part, so the end is dropped

parts.note: 17 11 is HARDY STORY; another of the right lengths is The Return of the Native, which supplies its last word

explanation.surface: Another Hardy novel provides the overture for a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the title as an instruction: the return of NATIVE is EVITAN, and its opening five letters name the show.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice stage musical about Eva Peron of Argentina.

clue.text: Walk in London taking "time" at prison

parts.note: bird is British slang for a prison sentence, from rhyming slang bird-lime, time
a cage is a place of confinement

explanation.surface: A stroll through London ending with a spell behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk' looks like a verb about strolling; it is part of a street name. Birdcage Walk is a road beside St James's Park in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The first word of the London street name Birdcage Walk, a crossword convention that lets one word stand for a fuller place name.

clue.text: No royal article these days

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for a noun meaning the present age

parts.note: a commoner is anyone not of royal or noble birth
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A remark that nowadays there are no royal stories in the papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the secular name for the dating system of the present period, the age we live in now.

clue.text: Singer formally attired?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a famous American bass who sang Ol' Man River
second meaning, split in two: ceremonial gowns worn on the body

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second reading needs the word split into two words to describe someone dressed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Robeson was a famous bass-baritone; robes worn on the body is formal, ceremonial dress.

clue.text: A number in a vehicle counter

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
taken as written

explanation.surface: A figure on the display of a vehicle meter.
explanation.walkthrough: The first A goes in with the number: A plus C sits inside A BUS.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of beads on wires used for doing arithmetic, a calculating device.

clue.text: By keeping right with slightly painful foot, nails are nearer to hand in such a case

definitions.text: nails are nearer to hand in such a case

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

parts.note: taken as written, split around what it keeps
R is the abbreviation for right
achy means mildly sore; the puzzle's grid has I where its A belongs
a dactyl is a metrical foot, one long syllable then two short

explanation.surface: A podiatry note: someone with a sore foot keeps right, and their nails are close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The word is brachydactyly, from Greek brachys, short; the third letter is A, as ACHY gives.
explanation.definitionFit: Brachydactyly is the condition of having unusually short fingers and toes, so fingernails sit closer to the palm.

clue.text: I provide time before getting into 30

indicators.note: to get into something is to go inside it

parts.note: the answer to 30 is MOTOR, and a motor is a car
T is the abbreviation for time
ere is a poetic word for before

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of giving their time before climbing into a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' looks like an order word; it is ERE. The clue speaks in the first person as the answer would.
explanation.definitionFit: A caterer supplies food and drink for functions, so would say of themselves that they provide.

clue.text: See 20
Ship's party needing redemption to give to posterity

indicators.note: what needs redeeming has been pawned, so it is held inside the pawnbroker's keeping

parts.note: goods in pawn await redemption by their owner
SS stands for steamship
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A crew's celebration is so costly that the ship's party ends up pawned.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no ordinary container word: 'needing redemption' describes goods left with a pawnbroker, so the ship and the party sit inside the pawned state.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass down is to hand something on to later generations, leaving it to descendants.

clue.text: Pioneering message: batterer turned against soldier turned batterer

indicators.note: something turned is facing the opposite way, so it is read backwards

parts.note: a ram is a battering device
con means against, as in pros and cons
GI is an American soldier
a ram again

explanation.surface: A dispatch about an abuser who turned on a soldier, who in turn became violent.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'turned' signal a reversal, of RAM and of GI; the final batterer stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: A marconigram was an early wireless telegram, sent by Marconi's pioneering radio system.

clue.text: Duchy at 10 with smothered daughter

parts.note: Brabant is a historic duchy in the Low Countries; the puzzle's grid has I in place of its second A
10 read as the letters I and O

explanation.surface: A dukedom at number ten, with a daughter stifled.
explanation.walkthrough: Brabantio, spelt with A as the duchy Brabant gives; '10' is not a clue reference here but the look-alike letters IO.
explanation.definitionFit: Brabantio is Desdemona's father in Othello, and Othello smothers his wife Desdemona in the final act.

clue.text: Ride to far country by a philosopher

parts.note: a spin is a short ride in a car
Oz is Australia, a far country from Britain
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thinker takes a trip to a distant land.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is the informal name for Australia, about as far from Britain as a country gets.
explanation.definitionFit: Baruch Spinoza was a seventeenth-century Dutch rationalist philosopher, author of the Ethics.

clue.text: Rich man heard to make us laugh?

indicators.note: what is heard is judged by its sound rather than by its spelling

parts.note: to crease someone is British slang for making them laugh helplessly

explanation.surface: A wealthy man is reported to be funny enough to have us in stitches.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a joke that creases you up doubles you over laughing; 'crease us' runs together into the king's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus was the king of Lydia famed for his wealth, whence the phrase as rich as Croesus.

clue.text: Tough kisser?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: robust, able to endure hardship
second meaning: the captain whom the dying Nelson asked for a kiss at Trafalgar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kisser' is slang for the mouth, but here it is a person who kissed. The answer, with 11, also names the puzzle's theme of Thomas Hardy novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy means tough and resilient, and Captain Thomas Hardy kissed Nelson at Trafalgar after 'Kiss me, Hardy'.

clue.text: Our tender ego we rented out to go round hospital

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps the other
letters put out of place are scattered from their order

parts.note: taken as written, twenty letters to rearrange
H is the map sign for a hospital

explanation.surface: A sensitive soul complains that the rented-out ego now has to visit a hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble makes this clue wordplay only. The long run of words is all letters to rearrange, wrapped round the hospital sign.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this is his 1872 rural novel of the Mellstock church choir.

clue.text: All those women — run a mile!

parts.note: to hare is to run fast
M is the abbreviation for a mile

explanation.surface: A man faced with so many women decides to flee as far as he can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run a mile' is an idiom for avoiding something at all costs; split up, it gives HARE and M.
explanation.definitionFit: A harem is the group of wives and concubines belonging to one man, so a whole household of females.

clue.text: 40's done wrong: there's no more to be said

definitions.text: there's no more to be said

indicators.note: letters set out wrongly are in the incorrect order and must be rearranged

parts.note: 40 written as the word, with the S, then done, ten letters in all

explanation.surface: Someone protests that the clue 40 has been bungled, and refuses to discuss it further.
explanation.walkthrough: '40' looks like a reference to clue 40, but it is the number forty spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: End of story is an idiom used to close a discussion firmly, saying nothing further needs adding.

clue.text: Bar worker from street when there's light outside

indicators.note: a thing outside another surrounds it

parts.note: a taper is a thin candle used for lighting
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A pub employee comes in off the street once daylight has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' seems to mean daylight; it is a taper, a slender candle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tapster is an old word for someone who draws beer in a tavern, a barman.

clue.text: The county is below standard

indicators.note: in a down clue what is below comes later in the column, so this piece is written second

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that the shire is underperforming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'County' looks like a shire; in Shakespeare it is an old word for a count. In a down clue IS placed below PAR reads PAR then IS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Romeo and Juliet, Juliet's suitor Paris is called the County Paris, county being an old title for a count.

clue.text: Pirate's hat is possibly there with no chance of escape

definitions.note: names a noun, while the answer is the adjective describing it

indicators.note: possibly means in some other version, so the letters can be arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
someone cornered is trapped with no way out

explanation.surface: A pirate's hat might be hiding somewhere, with no way of getting out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the classic pirate's hat, the tricorne, is three-cornered.
explanation.definitionFit: The tricorne worn by pirates in illustrations has its brim turned up on three sides, forming three points.

clue.text: See 28
Writer gave name to flower

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Roald, author of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
second meaning: Anders, the Swedish botanist commemorated in a garden bloom

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests one writer naming a flower; in fact two different men share the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory; the botanist Anders Dahl is commemorated by the dahlia.

clue.text: Marx turns up with Lady Chat

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up flips the word so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: Harpo Marx, the silent one of the Marx Brothers

explanation.surface: One of the Marx Brothers drops in for a conversation with a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Harpo was the harp-playing, mute Marx brother; Oprah named her production company Harpo, her name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Oprah Winfrey is the American television host, the leading lady of the chat show genre.

clue.text: Language spoken in marriage?

indicators.note: something spoken is taken by its sound, not its letters

parts.note: marriage is a tie, the bond in which a couple is joined

explanation.surface: Which tongue do a husband and wife talk to each other?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Language spoken in' looks like one phrase asking where a language is used; 'spoken' is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Thai is the official language of Thailand, a tonal language of South-East Asia.

clue.text: It's bad for the farm being a summer bird, doctor holds

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside
bad letters are out of order and need putting right

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
MD, Doctor of Medicine
a summer is one who sums, so being a summer is adding
a crow is a bird

explanation.surface: A summer visitor bird is bad news for the farm, and a vet keeps hold of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble makes this wordplay only. 'Summer' looks like the season; it is one who sums, so being one is ADDING.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this 1874 novel follows Bathsheba Everdene and her three suitors.

clue.text: Appearance of champion in pink paper

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: the Financial Times, a British newspaper printed on pink paper
an ace is an expert or champion

explanation.surface: A winner turns up in the business pages of the press.
explanation.walkthrough: The pink paper is the Financial Times, Britain's financial daily, known by its salmon-coloured pages.
explanation.definitionFit: A facet is one side or aspect of something, the way it presents itself from one angle.

clue.text: Playing footy with 19, one who will throw game

indicators.note: letters at play are moving about freely rather than holding their order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the answer to 19 down
a caster is one who casts, or throws
bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A man plays football alongside his harem, but he is ready to throw the match.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble makes this wordplay only. 'Throw game' suggests match-fixing; it is a caster, then the card game. Footy is British slang for football.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this 1886 novel tells of Michael Henchard, who sold his wife.

clue.text: Dr Hill's vehicle

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a doctor
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A doctor named Hill shows off his car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dr Hill' looks like one person; it is two pieces, a doctor and then a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Motor is an informal British word for a car, as in a nice motor.

clue.text: See 29
Something like an umbrella needed to hit a six

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the ribbed, stretched membrane of a flying mammal looks like an opened umbrella
second meaning: a cricket bat must be swung to hit the ball for six

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a six is a hit clearing the boundary without bouncing; read as two words with the apostrophe ignored, the answer is that stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin stretched over the long finger bones of the animal resembles the fabric stretched over umbrella spokes.

clue.text: Food and wages can be driven below surface

parts.note: grub is informal for food
screw is old British slang for wages

explanation.surface: Pay and rations are being pushed down under the waterline.
explanation.walkthrough: Screw as wages is dated British slang; the definition describes the item by what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: A grub screw has no head, so it can be turned in until it sits flush with or under the material's face.

clue.text: Flirts at dance in playground?

parts.note: to toy with someone is to flirt
a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: Teenagers flirting at a school disco held out on the playground.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as playful: a shop full of toys is a ground for play.
explanation.definitionFit: A store selling playthings is jokingly a place of play, as children treat it as one.

clue.text: Shakespearean's letters sound American

parts.note: post is the mail, letters delivered
a hum is a low sound
US for United States, so American

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare scholar's correspondence has a transatlantic ring to it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters sound American' reads as a comment on spelling; it is three pieces in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Posthumus Leonatus is the hero of Cymbeline, Imogen's husband, a character from one of Shakespeare's plays.

clue.text: From the first I love to follow article and then throw it away

indicators.note: what follows comes afterwards, so this pair is placed at the end

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
to bin something is to throw it away
taken as written
love is nil in tennis scoring, the letter O

explanation.surface: A lover's confession: one devoted reading of an article, then binning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Throw it away' gives two words, BIN IT; I and O go after A plus that.
explanation.definitionFit: Ab initio is Latin for from the beginning, used for starting something over from its origin.

clue.text: Humorous writer is without editor after backing little ditch for towns across the water

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: a fosse is a ditch; a fossette is a small one

indicators.note: to be without in the old sense is to be outside, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: James Thurber, the American humorist
ed is the abbreviation for editor
villes is French for towns, across the Channel

explanation.surface: A comic author is missing an editor once a small ditch has been dug out for some foreign towns.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble makes this wordplay only. 'Without' is old usage for outside, so the humorist wraps round the editor. 'Across the water' points to France.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this 1891 novel follows a milkmaid seduced and later hanged.

clue.text: A manner of speaking in which I speak of myself in body

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a star is a heavenly body
how a stutterer would say me, with the first sound repeated

explanation.surface: Describing a way of talking where the speaker refers to himself in the flesh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body' suggests the human body; it is a heavenly body. The clue enacts its own answer: the speaker trips over the word for himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A stammer is a speech impediment with involuntary repetition of sounds, a way of talking.

clue.text: Suitable words on grave in untidy heap

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
an untidy pile is jumbled out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a grave is a pit dug in the ground

explanation.surface: The fitting inscription for a headstone found lying in a messy pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Words on grave' looks like the whole definition, but 'grave' is needed as wordplay; the definition is just the opening pair.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitaph is the brief commemorative inscription carved for the dead, words chosen to fit a life.

clue.text: Passenger (sorry, customer) is being processed

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one travelling by rail, whom rail companies now insist on calling a customer
second meaning: under way, in progress

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket mocks British railway companies for calling their passengers customers; both kinds are people on board a train.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail passenger is someone on board a carriage, and matters in train are already under way and in progress.

clue.text: Alice is upset — remove frock?

indicators.note: something upset has been knocked over and its parts scattered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Alice is upset and wants to take her dress off.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'is' as part of 'Alice is upset'; it is half of the letters. The frock is a cleric's, not Alice's dress.
explanation.definitionFit: To laicise is to make secular or remove from clerical status, as defrocking a priest returns him to the laity.

clue.text: Changing Blair to Brown needed central intelligence

indicators.note: a change of one figure for another swaps some parts while keeping the rest

parts.note: Gordon Brown keeps only his outer letters B, R and N
Tony Blair keeps only his central letters

explanation.surface: Replacing Tony Blair with Gordon Brown as British prime minister required brains at the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair keeps his middle, A and I; Brown provides the outside letters around it. Brown succeeded Blair as prime minister in 2007.
explanation.definitionFit: The brain is the organ at the centre of the nervous system where thinking happens.

clue.text: People's tips are in order: like one of them?

indicators.note: things in something are held inside it

parts.note: to bid is to order or command

indicators.note: tips are the extreme ends, so only the first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Everyone's tips are fine, which makes a person what exactly?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' points back to 'People': a person walks on two feet. 'In order' reads as tidy; it is a container signal then BID.
explanation.definitionFit: Biped as an adjective means two-footed, which describes any human being, since humans walk on two legs.

clue.text: A little paper on holiday

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount, as in not a whit
The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: Taking a small newspaper along while on vacation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid paper; 'a little' is WHIT, as in not a whit.
explanation.definitionFit: Whitsun is the Christian festival of Pentecost, and Whit Monday was long a British bank holiday.

clue.text: Sulky start of reporter's request?

indicators.note: a reporter tells us what is said, so the sound is what counts

parts.note: a petition is a formal request; its first two syllables are pe-tish

explanation.surface: A journalist begins a request in a grumpy mood.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the opening of the word for the request is wanted: the first two syllables of petition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pettish means peevish and petulant, given to small fits of bad temper, as a sulking person is.

clue.text: Predatory start for predator's predatory movement

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening, so only the front is kept

parts.note: the opening two letters
an owl is a bird of prey

explanation.surface: A hunter's first stalking step on the move.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word appears three times; each one does a different job, and only the last pair is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To prowl is to move about stealthily in search of prey, as a hunting animal does.

clue.text: Apple once given to queen at a dogs' home

parts.note: pome is an old word for an apple
a rani is an Indian queen
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone once gave a queen an apple at an animal shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs' home' suggests an animal rescue centre; it is the homeland of a breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pomerania, a region on the Baltic coast, gave its name to the Pomeranian, a small fluffy breed.

clue.text: Philosophy of a moralist in trouble

indicators.note: something in trouble is disordered and thrown about

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A thinker's belief system belongs to a moralist who is in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In trouble' reads as one phrase, but 'in' belongs to the letters and 'trouble' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rationalism is the school of thought holding reason, not the senses, as the source of knowledge.

clue.text: Make fun of foreign journey

parts.note: de is French and Spanish for of
a ride is a trip

explanation.surface: Mocking someone else's trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make fun of' looks like the whole definition; 'of' is needed for its foreign version, DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride is to mock or ridicule someone, treating them with scorn.

clue.text: Ambassador in 2 has nothing left among passions

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: the number written as a word
HE, His Excellency, the title of an ambassador
nothing is zero, the letter O

indicators.note: something among others is placed within them

parts.note: a dander is a temper, as in getting your dander up
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An envoy at number two has nothing remaining amid the strong feelings.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble makes this wordplay only. '2' looks like a clue reference but is just the number spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names these entries as Hardy stories, and this 1887 novel is set among the cider-makers of Little Hintock.
